steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for an NLP paper proposing a plug-and-play, tunable policy planner that helps LLM-powered dialogue agents handle proactive dialogues (negotiation, emotional support, tutoring): the problem, limits of existing policy planning methods, our framework, and our evaluation approach.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
Introduction
- LLM dialogue agents are good but passive; struggle with proactive dialogues
- Dialogue policy planning: pre-LLM corpus-based methods, recent prompt-based methods
- Remaining challenges (three)
- Our approach: PPDPP plug-in, SFT + self-play RL with AI feedback
- LLM-based interactive evaluation + experiments

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
Introduction
- LLM-powered dialogue agents
  - e.g. ChatGPT, Vicuna, LLaMA2-Chat
  - strong context understanding + response generation on various dialogue problems
  - but trained to passively follow instructions -> prioritize accommodating user intention
  - struggle with proactive dialogue problems: agent must strategically take initiative to steer conversation to an anticipated goal
  - examples: negotiation, emotional support, tutoring
- Dialogue policy planning
  - key: improve agents' policy planning = deciding what actions to take to achieve specific goals during dynamic interaction with the user
  - pre-LLM: corpus-based learning, dialogue act prediction
    - rely on static human-annotated dialogues; don't optimize long-term goal
  - LLMs: fine-tuning whole system per application unrealistic and costly
  - recent prompt-based methods (Figure 1 (a)) prompt frozen actor LLM to:
    - self-think strategy planning each turn
    - or generate AI feedback on whole dialogue history to iteratively improve planning for a certain case
- Challenges
  1) LLMs poor at planning effective policy with zero-/few-shot prompting -> improvement limited by frozen actor LLM's planning ability
  2) iterative refinement approaches lack transferability: many rounds of self-play simulation per new case; impractical in real world
  3) evaluation: turn-level response quality vs fixed reference responses; can't automatically assess policy planning = effectiveness + efficiency of goal achievement over multi-turn conversation
- Our approach: Plug-and-Play Dialogue Policy Planner (PPDPP)
  - tunable language model plug-in that strategizes LLMs
  - Figure 1 (b): policy agent predicts next-turn dialogue strategy for the dialogue agent
  - first supervised fine-tuning on available human-annotated corpora
  - self-play: two LLMs (assistant, user) with case background info role-play, simulating dynamic multi-turn environment
  - distinct, often competing goals (negotiation: buyer wants better price, seller wants higher price)
  - third LLM = reward model: goal-oriented verbal feedback -> scalar rewards for RL
  - at goal or max turn: RL tunes policy agent on interaction data + AI feedback
  - benefits: more adaptable to new cases than prompt-based; switch plug-in across applications without affecting the LLM's abilities
- Evaluation and experiments
  - LLM-based interactive evaluation using LLM user simulators + reward models
  - measures success rate and average number of turns to reach goals
  - three proactive dialogue problems: negotiation, emotional support, tutoring
  - PPDPP outperforms existing LLM-based dialogue systems; leads conversations to goal effectively and efficiently

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Introduction
Dialogue agents powered by large language models (LLMs), for example ChatGPT, Vicuna and LLaMA2-Chat, have shown that they are very good at understanding context and generating responses in various dialogue problems. But LLMs are trained to passively follow the instructions of users, so dialogue agents that are built on them usually prioritize accommodating what the user intends. Because of this, LLM-powered dialogue agents often have trouble with proactive dialogue problems, where the dialogue agent has to strategically take the initiative and steer the conversation towards an anticipated goal. Examples are negotiation, emotional support, and tutoring.

In these scenarios, the key is to improve the dialogue policy planning capability of LLM-powered dialogue agents. Dialogue policy planning is the process of deciding which actions the dialogue agent should take so that it effectively achieves specific goals during the dynamic interactions with the user. Before LLMs, researchers mostly used corpus-based learning approaches that do the dialogue policy planning by predicting dialogue acts. But these approaches depend heavily on static dialogues annotated by humans, and they do not optimize the long-term goal of the conversation. Now that we have LLMs, it is also unrealistic and costly to fine-tune the whole dialogue system for every specific application. So recent works, as shown in Figure 1 (a), look at prompt-based policy planning methods. These methods prompt a frozen actor LLM to either do self-thinking of strategy planning at each turn, or to generate AI feedback given the whole dialogue history so that the dialogue policy planning for a certain case is improved iteratively.

These methods are effective in improving dialogue policy planning, but there are still several challenges. 1) LLMs are not good at planning effective dialogue policy with zero-shot or few-shot prompting schemes. So how much better the agent gets at accomplishing the goal is limited by how well the frozen actor LLM can plan. 2) The existing approaches that are based on iterative refinement are not transferable, because they need multiple rounds of self-play dialogue simulations for every new case to plan a good strategy for it, and this is impractical in real-world applications. 3) Existing studies usually evaluate dialogue agents with turn-level measurements of response quality that are based on fixed reference responses. But these evaluation protocols cannot automatically assess the policy planning capability of the dialogue agent, which depends on how effectively and efficiently the goal is achieved in multi-turn conversations.

- Our approach: Plug-and-Play Dialogue Policy Planner (PPDPP)
  - tunable language model plug-in that strategizes LLMs
  - Figure 1 (b): policy agent predicts next-turn dialogue strategy for the dialogue agent
  - first supervised fine-tuning on available human-annotated corpora
  - self-play: two LLMs (assistant, user) with case background info role-play, simulating dynamic multi-turn environment
  - distinct, often competing goals (negotiation: buyer wants better price, seller wants higher price)
  - third LLM = reward model: goal-oriented verbal feedback -> scalar rewards for RL
  - at goal or max turn: RL tunes policy agent on interaction data + AI feedback
  - benefits: more adaptable to new cases than prompt-based; switch plug-in across applications without affecting the LLM's abilities
- Evaluation and experiments
  - LLM-based interactive evaluation using LLM user simulators + reward models
  - measures success rate and average number of turns to reach goals
  - three proactive dialogue problems: negotiation, emotional support, tutoring
  - PPDPP outperforms existing LLM-based dialogue systems; leads conversations to goal effectively and efficiently

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Introduction
Dialogue agents powered by large language models (LLMs), for example ChatGPT, Vicuna and LLaMA2-Chat, have shown that they are very good at understanding context and generating responses in various dialogue problems. But LLMs are trained to passively follow the instructions of users, so dialogue agents that are built on them usually prioritize accommodating what the user intends. Because of this, LLM-powered dialogue agents often have trouble with proactive dialogue problems, where the dialogue agent has to strategically take the initiative and steer the conversation towards an anticipated goal. Examples are negotiation, emotional support, and tutoring.

In these scenarios, the key is to improve the dialogue policy planning capability of LLM-powered dialogue agents. Dialogue policy planning is the process of deciding which actions the dialogue agent should take so that it effectively achieves specific goals during the dynamic interactions with the user. Before LLMs, researchers mostly used corpus-based learning approaches that do the dialogue policy planning by predicting dialogue acts. But these approaches depend heavily on static dialogues annotated by humans, and they do not optimize the long-term goal of the conversation. Now that we have LLMs, it is also unrealistic and costly to fine-tune the whole dialogue system for every specific application. So recent works, as shown in Figure 1 (a), look at prompt-based policy planning methods. These methods prompt a frozen actor LLM to either do self-thinking of strategy planning at each turn, or to generate AI feedback given the whole dialogue history so that the dialogue policy planning for a certain case is improved iteratively.

These methods are effective in improving dialogue policy planning, but there are still several challenges. 1) LLMs are not good at planning effective dialogue policy with zero-shot or few-shot prompting schemes. So how much better the agent gets at accomplishing the goal is limited by how well the frozen actor LLM can plan. 2) The existing approaches that are based on iterative refinement are not transferable, because they need multiple rounds of self-play dialogue simulations for every new case to plan a good strategy for it, and this is impractical in real-world applications. 3) Existing studies usually evaluate dialogue agents with turn-level measurements of response quality that are based on fixed reference responses. But these evaluation protocols cannot automatically assess the policy planning capability of the dialogue agent, which depends on how effectively and efficiently the goal is achieved in multi-turn conversations.

To deal with these challenges, we introduce a new dialogue policy planning paradigm which strategizes LLMs with a tunable language model plug-in, and we call it Plug-and-Play Dialogue Policy Planner (PPDPP). As shown in Figure 1 (b), PPDPP is the policy agent that predicts the dialogue strategy at the next turn for the dialogue agent. It can first be fine-tuned in a supervised way with human-annotated corpora that are available. Then we use the self-play paradigm, where we prompt two LLMs (an assistant and a user) with various case background information to do a role-playing conversation. This conversation simulates the dynamic environment of multi-turn interactions between the dialogue agent and the real user. For each case the two LLMs each get distinct goals that often compete (for example in negotiation dialogues the buyer wants a more favorable price, and the seller wants a higher price). At the same time, a third LLM is the reward model, and it gives goal-oriented verbal feedback that indicates whether the goal is achieved. This feedback is transformed into scalar rewards that are used for reinforcement learning (RL). When the goal or the maximum conversation turn is reached, we use an RL algorithm to tune the policy agent further with the interaction data we collected and the goal-oriented AI feedback. This way the LLM-powered dialogue agent is more adaptable to various new cases than prompt-based approaches, and it can also be used across diverse applications just by switching the tuned plug-in, without affecting the LLM's exceptional context understanding and response generation capabilities.

Traditional turn-level response evaluation metrics have limitations, so we also propose an LLM-based interactive evaluation approach which uses the LLM-based user simulators and reward models that we introduced above. With this approach we can simulate diverse user-assistant interactions and assess both the success rate and the average number of turns for achieving the designated goals. We do extensive experiments on three different proactive dialogue problems, which are negotiation, emotional support, and tutoring dialogues. The experimental results show that the proposed PPDPP framework is better than existing LLM-based dialogue systems, and that PPDPP can lead the conversations to the designated goal effectively and efficiently.

Introduction

However, since LLMs are trained to passively follow users' instructions, dialogue agents built on them typically prioritize accommodating the user's intention. As a result, LLM-powered dialogue agents often struggle with proactive dialogue problems, which require the dialogue agent to strategically take the initiative and steer the conversation towards an anticipated goal [7], such as negotiation [8], emotional support [9,10], and tutoring [11].

In such scenarios, the key is to improve the dialogue policy planning capability of LLM-powered dialogue agents, i.e., the process of deciding what actions the dialogue agent should take to effectively achieve specific goals during the dynamic interactions with the user. In the pre-LLM era, researchers mainly used corpus-based learning approaches to conduct dialogue policy planning via dialogue act prediction [12,13,14,15,16,17]. However, such approaches rely heavily on static human-annotated dialogues and fail to optimize the long-term goal of the conversation. With the advent of LLMs, it also becomes unrealistic and costly to fine-tune the whole dialogue system for every specific application. Although these methods are effective in improving dialogue policy planning, several challenges remain. 1) LLMs fall short of planning effective dialogue policy with zero-shot or few-shot prompting schemes [19], so the improvement in accomplishing the goal is limited by the planning capability of the frozen actor LLM. 2) Existing approaches based on iterative refinement [21,22] lack transferability, since multiple rounds of self-play dialogue simulations are required for every new case to plan a satisfactory strategy for it, which is impractical in real-world applications. 3) Existing studies typically evaluate dialogue agents with turn-level response quality measurements based on fixed reference responses. However, these evaluation protocols cannot automatically assess the policy planning capability of the dialogue agent, which is determined by the effectiveness and efficiency of goal achievement in multi-turn conversations.

To tackle these challenges, we introduce a novel dialogue policy planning paradigm that strategizes LLMs with a tunable language model plug-in, named Plug-and-Play Dialogue Policy Planner (PPDPP). As shown in Figure 1 (b), PPDPP acts as the policy agent that predicts the dialogue strategy at the next turn for the dialogue agent, and it can first be supervisedly fine-tuned with available human-annotated corpora. We then employ the self-play paradigm, prompting two LLMs (an assistant and a user) with various case background information to carry out a role-playing conversation that simulates the dynamic environment of multi-turn interactions between the dialogue agent and the real user. For each case, the two LLMs are given distinct, often competing goals (e.g., in negotiation dialogues, the buyer seeks a more favorable price, whereas the seller wants a higher price). Meanwhile, a third LLM acts as the reward model and provides goal-oriented verbal feedback indicating the goal achievement, which is transformed into scalar rewards for reinforcement learning (RL). When the goal or the maximum conversation turn is reached, we use an RL algorithm to further tune the policy agent with the collected interaction data and the goal-oriented AI feedback. In this way, the LLM-powered dialogue agent not only shows more adaptability to various new cases than prompt-based approaches, but can also be used across diverse applications simply by switching the tuned plug-in, without affecting the LLM's exceptional capabilities of context understanding and response generation.

To overcome the limitation of traditional turn-level response evaluation metrics, we further propose an LLM-based interactive evaluation approach that uses the LLM-based user simulators and reward models introduced above. This approach simulates diverse user-assistant interactions to assess both the success rate and the average number of turns needed to achieve the designated goals. We conduct extensive experiments on three different proactive dialogue problems: negotiation, emotional support, and tutoring dialogues. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of the proposed PPDPP framework over existing LLM-based dialogue systems, showing that PPDPP can effectively and efficiently lead conversations to the designated goal.
